name: Patrol Route
description:
What something does when it is not hunting anybody: roam near where it belongs. It is the other half of movement.pursuit_agent, and the reason both exist is that a world where enemies stand perfectly still until they see you is a world of statues — the moment before being noticed is most of what makes being noticed feel like anything.

HOME IS WHERE IT SPAWNED, not a route a designer drew. A patrol path is content, and content that has to be authored per enemy per level is content that will not be authored, so the default is a radius around the tile the unit started on and a designer who wants a real route supplies waypoints instead. Either way it is an ANCHOR: a wanderer that drifts is a wanderer that ends up somewhere it was never meant to guard.

It yields immediately and completely to combat.aggro_table: a unit with a target is not patrolling, and this stops rather than fighting the pursuer for the same body. Where no aggro component is in the build it patrols unconditionally, which is honest — nothing in that build knows how to notice anything. It emits movement.moveExecuted, the same event a tactical move and a pursuit both use, so combat.unit_roster stays the only thing that writes a position and no third event is invented for the third way of walking.

It does not own the pace of a chase, the decision to chase, or where the body IS. Those are the pursuer's, the aggro table's, and the roster's.

NOT world.mob_patrol, which the catalogue already has and which is a different thing wearing a similar word. That one is a platformer package: it OWNS its mobs — it spawns them, paces them along a surface, turns them at ledges and resolves contact as a stomp or a hazard — and it depends on movement.character_body because all of that is side-scroller physics. This owns no entities at all. It moves units that combat.unit_roster already holds, on a tile grid, and resolves nothing: a hit is combat.contact_attack's and noticing is combat.aggro_table's. Two components can both be called patrol and still be a package and a verb.

implementations.note: Implemented in the consuming application; not verifiable from this repository.

inputs.name: radius
inputs.description: How far from home a patroller will wander, in tiles. It is an anchor and not a drift: without one, a roamer performs a random walk and a random walk has no home, so after two minutes the thing guarding the bridge is in the woods.

inputs.name: tilesPerSecond
inputs.description: Roaming pace, deliberately separate from movement.pursuit_agent's and deliberately slower by default. The change of pace when something notices you is the clearest signal in the whole encounter, and one shared number would throw it away.

inputs.name: pauseSeconds
inputs.description: How long a patroller waits at the end of a leg before choosing the next one. Continuous motion reads as a machine on rails; the pause is what makes it read as an animal.

inputs.name: waypoints
inputs.description: An authored route per unit id, as {unitId: [{x, y}, ...]}, walked in order and looped. Where a unit has one it is used instead of the radius, so a guard can be given a beat while everything else in the level roams. A named unit with an empty route roams rather than standing still, because an empty list is far more likely to be a level that was not finished than a deliberate statue.

outputs.name: patrolling
outputs.description: Which units are currently roaming, and the tile each is heading for. A measurement of zero while a build visibly contains idle enemies is the finding, and without this it is invisible.

outputs.name: homeOf
outputs.description: The anchor tile each patroller is roaming around. Published because it is decided here — from wherever the unit spawned — and a level that wants to check its guards are guarding the right places has no other way to ask.

provenance: Asked for alongside combat.aggro_table: "we want the wolves to kind of roam an area before going for the player once they can see them".
